content: Each year, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reviews the recommended immunization schedule for children and adolescents. This review ensures that the schedule reflects updates in vaccine formulations from manufacturers and incorporates revised recommendations for the use of licensed vaccines, including newly approved ones. In 2003, a catch-up immunization schedule was introduced for children and adolescents who start vaccinations late or are more than one month behind. This schedule remains unchanged. The schedule specifies the minimum ages and intervals between doses for all routinely recommended vaccines for children and adolescents. Hepatitis B Vaccine The recommended minimum age for the final dose in the hepatitis B vaccination series has been updated. The last dose should not be administered before 24 weeks of age, replacing the previous recommendation of not administering it before 6 months of age. Adolescent Tetanus and Diphtheria Toxoids (Td) Vaccine The recommended age range for the adolescent Td vaccine has been updated. Vaccination is now preferred at ages 11–12 years, with ages 13–18 years serving as a catch-up interval. Clarifications on Final Doses Clarifications have been added to the footnotes regarding the timing of the final doses in the vaccination series for the diphtheria and tetanus toxoids and acellular pertussis (DTaP) vaccine, Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) conjugate vaccine, and pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV). The final dose in the DTaP series should be administered at age 4 years or older. The final doses in the Hib and PCV series should be administered at age 12 months or older. Influenza Vaccine Healthy children aged 6–23 months are encouraged to receive the influenza vaccine during the 2003–2004 influenza season, as this age group is at significantly increased risk for influenza-related hospitalizations. Starting in fall 2004, annual influenza vaccination will be recommended for children aged 6–23 months. An updated immunization schedule for July–December 2004 will reflect this change. A live, attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV), administered intranasally, was approved in June 2003 for use in the United States. For healthy individuals aged 5–49 years, LAIV is an acceptable alternative to the intramuscular trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine (TIV). Vaccine Information Statements The National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act mandates that healthcare providers give parents or patients copies of Vaccine Information Statements (VIS) before administering each dose of vaccines listed in the schedule. Detailed recommendations for vaccine use can be found in manufacturers' package inserts, ACIP statements, and the 2003 Red Book. ACIP statements for each recommended childhood vaccine are available for viewing, downloading, and printing. Hepatitis B Vaccine (HepB) All infants should receive the first dose of the HepB vaccine shortly after birth and before hospital discharge. If the mother is HBsAg-negative, the first dose may be given by age 2 months. Only monovalent HepB vaccine should be used for the birth dose. Monovalent or combination vaccines containing HepB may be used to complete the series. If a birth dose is given, up to 4 doses of the vaccine may be administered. The second dose should be given at least 4 weeks after the first dose, except for combination vaccines, which cannot be administered before age 6 weeks. The third dose should be given at least 16 weeks after the first dose and at least 8 weeks after the second dose. The final dose (third or fourth) should not be administered before 24 weeks of age. Infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers should receive 0.5 mL of hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth at separate sites. The second dose is recommended at age 1–2 months, and the final dose should not be administered before 24 weeks of age. These infants should be tested for HBsAg and anti-HBs at age 9–15 months. Infants born to mothers with unknown HBsAg status should receive the first dose of the HepB vaccine series within 12 hours of birth. Maternal blood should be drawn as soon as possible to determine HBsAg status. If the test is positive, the infant should receive HBIG as soon as possible, no later than age 1 week. The second dose is recommended at age 1–2 months, and the final dose should not be administered before 24 weeks of age. Diphtheria and Tetanus Toxoids and Acellular Pertussis Vaccine (DTaP) The fourth dose of DTaP may be administered at age 12 months, provided that 6 months have elapsed since the third dose and the child is unlikely to return at age 15–18 months. The final dose in the series should be given at age 4 years or older. Tetanus and diphtheria toxoids (Td) are recommended at age 11–12 years if at least 5 years have passed since the last dose of a tetanus and diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccine. Subsequent routine Td boosters are recommended every 10 years. Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) Conjugate Vaccine Hib vaccine is generally not recommended for children aged 5 years or older. Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) For children who received an all-IPV or all-oral poliovirus (OPV) series, a fourth dose is not necessary if the third dose was given at age 4 years or older. If both OPV and IPV were given as part of a series, a total of 4 doses should be administered, regardless of the child’s current age. IPV is generally not recommended for individuals aged 18 years or older. Measles, Mumps, and Rubella Vaccine (MMR) The second dose of MMR is routinely recommended at age 4–6 years but may be given earlier if desired. Varicella Vaccine (VAR) A 2-dose series should be administered to all susceptible adolescents aged 13 years or older. Reporting Adverse Reactions Clinically significant adverse events following vaccination should be reported to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS). Guidance on completing a VAERS form is available online or by telephone at 800-822-7967. Disease Reporting Suspected cases of vaccine-preventable diseases should be reported to state or local health departments. Additional Information Further information about vaccines, including precautions, contraindications, and vaccine shortages, is available online or through the National Immunization Information Hotline at 800-232-2522 (English) or 800-232-0233 (Spanish).
